draft.title: River regulation
card: River regulation means people control how much water flows down a river and when. Dams, weirs and straightened channels are the main tools.
A dam holds back water in a large storage. A weir is a low wall across a river that raises the water level and slows the flow. Straightening a channel lets water move through faster.
Regulation supplies water for towns and farms. It can also reduce flooding of homes and paddocks downstream.
Wetlands and many fish depend on natural floods, which fill wetlands and trigger breeding. Regulation can reduce or change these floods, as it has on the Murray-Darling river system.
draft.remember: Regulation gives people steady water and less flooding, but it can change the floods that nature relies on.

opts: A low wall across a river that raises the water level
A large storage that holds back water behind a high wall
A channel cut straight so that water moves faster
A wetland that fills when a river floods
a.why: A weir is a low wall across a river that raises the water level and slows the flow. A dam is the large storage, so it is the most tempting wrong answer, but it holds back much more water.
a.clue: Think of a low wall, not a big storage.

b.q: Farms along a regulated river in the Murray-Darling now get steady water all year. Downstream, a wetland rarely floods and its fish breed less often. What explains the change at the wetland?
opts: Regulation has reduced the floods the wetland needs
Regulation has made floods bigger and more frequent
Farms have straightened the wetland's natural channel
Regulation has stopped water reaching the farms
b.why: The wetland and its fish depend on natural floods, and regulation can reduce them. Bigger floods are the opposite of what happened here, since the wetland now rarely floods.
b.clue: What do wetlands and fish need that dams and weirs can change?

a.best: A low wall across a river that raises the water level

b.best: Regulation has reduced the floods the wetland needs

b.q: A large dam is built upstream of a wetland on a Murray-Darling river. It stores water for farms and holds back high flows. What is the likely effect on the wetland?
opts: Floods that fill the wetland become smaller or rarer
Its fish breed more often because flows are steadier
Floods become bigger because the dam slows the river
It stays the same, since dams change only upstream flow
b.why: The dam holds back high flows, so the floods that fill the wetland can become smaller or rarer. Steadier flows may sound helpful, but many fish need natural floods to trigger breeding, so they may breed less, not more.
b.clue: What do fish in wetlands need to start breeding?
